issues.why: Two atomic-write implementations in one feature. write_atomic uses a fixed '<name>.tmp' (not unique, no fsync), and a concurrent writer or crash leaves a stale .tmp. _write uses mkstemp, fsync and cleanup. The weaker copy is used for review artifacts (master.json, meta.json).
issues.fix: Move _write into mb_team_shared (or review_core) as one write_atomic(path, text) using mkstemp+fsync, and use it from both.

issues.why: main catches KeyError, AttributeError and TypeError and prints them as '[team-review] <msg>' with exit 2. Programming bugs are reported as an opaque one-word message ('KeyError: x') with no traceback, which hides defects in review.
issues.fix: Catch only ReviewError, RenderError and CalledProcessError. Validate expected inputs explicitly and raise ReviewError at those points.

issues.why: Same catch-all of KeyError and ValueError around render hides bugs as a user error.
issues.fix: Narrow it to RenderError. Convert expected KeyError/ValueError (config lookups) into RenderError where raised.

issues.why: Unparsable subprocess output is silently collapsed. _json returns {} on invalid JSON, so a crashed script looks like a clean empty result; status.py skips lines with 'continue'. gate.py line 76 handles this correctly by reporting 'unreadable output' - the others do not.
issues.fix: Have _json return an error marker, or raise TeamError that includes returncode and stderr, in the same form gate.py:76 already uses.

issues.file: scripts/mb_lock_queue.py (whole file, 299 lines) vs scripts/_lib.sh:mb_lock_acquire and mb_team_state.locked
issues.why: Three locking mechanisms in one repo: _lib.sh owner-marker mkdir lock, flock in mb_team_state.locked, and the mb-lock.sh ticket queue with its own pid/start-time liveness check. The mb-lock design is justified for fair queueing of host-wide resources. But the flock in locked() is a fourth, differing mutex for team.json. It is acceptable as a single-file critical section, but it does not reuse the repo's reclaim logic. mb_lock_queue.py sits at the 300-line SRP limit and mixes process liveness, ticket queue, status rendering and 7 op_* handlers.
issues.fix: Record in a comment, or in the ADR, why flock is kept for team.json (kernel releases it on death, so no reclaim is needed). Split liveness helpers (proc_start, alive, holder_alive) and status_of into mb_lock_liveness.py when the file next grows.

issues.why: Close to the 300-line SRP threshold. status.py mixes gathering, board-text formatting and CLI.
issues.fix: Extract the formatting from status.py to a module if it grows past 300.

issues.why: The review-gate JSON verdict is validated with a try/raise ValueError/except ValueError idiom (control flow via exception, with a message that is separate from the error).
issues.fix: Use json.loads in try, then a plain isinstance check with its own error branch.

issues.why: ADVISORY_RULES is a single-element tuple, one constant for a single value. It is fine, but it is also dead flexibility if no other advisory rule is planned.
issues.fix: Keep it, or inline it if no second rule is expected.

issues.why: Each CLI repeats the same pattern: argparse, ConfigError catch printing '[prefix] msg' lines, return 2. Seven copies of the ConfigError handling block (3+ copies).
issues.fix: Add shared.report_config_error(prefix, exc) -> int to mb_team_shared and call it from each main (about 3 lines saved each).

summary: No blockers or majors. The design is mostly clean and modular (no file over 300 lines; Clean Architecture direction held). Main concerns: duplicated and unequal atomic-write helpers, over-broad exception catches that hide bugs as user errors, silent swallowing of unparsable subprocess output, plus locking-mechanism overlap that needs a documented rationale.
